case_study_insert.main_stem: Dunmore Paper and Cartons (DPC) is a private limited company in the packaging manufacturing sector, employing a workforce of 100. Founded in 2010 by Bryn Dunmore, the business supplies recycled cardboard cartons to food and electronics firms and operates a flat structure with autocratic leadership. DPC plans to invest $840,000 in a recycled-cardboard line using eco-friendly inks, financed by a $480,000 bank loan and $360,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.50 a unit and a selling price of $13.50, and currently produces 100,000 units a year. DPC faces a high defect rate in carton printing and increasing complaints about late deliveries.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Operations Report — Q1 2025: The carton line produced 25,000 units last quarter with a defect rate of 2.9%, down from 4.4% a year earlier. Late-delivery complaints fell from 37 to 16 per month. Average order lead time is 3.7 days. A survey of 550 purchasers found that 63% would pay up to $0.40 more for cartons printed with eco-friendly inks, and 49% check packaging credentials before placing orders. A training review shows 24 of 100 staff have not been trained on the new printing presses; college courses cost $950 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Dunmore Paper and Cartons for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, increasing borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.4% from $13.25 to $14.10 per hour from April 2026, raising total wage costs. (3) Paper pulp and eco-ink input costs have risen 9.8% year-on-year, while consumer spending on packaged goods grew 2.2%.

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for DPC of using retained profit instead of the bank loan to fund the recycled-cardboard line.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using $360,000 of retained profit incurs no interest or repayments, protecting DPC's cash flow while it already carries $300,000 of fixed costs a year. With the base interest rate at 5.25%, interest on a $480,000 bank loan would be an avoidable drain; internal funds keep the whole $6.00 contribution on each carton in the business to absorb the 9.8% rise in pulp and eco-ink costs without pushing the $13.50 price above what food and electronics firms will pay.

Point 2: Retained profit requires no collateral, so the $840,000 recycled-cardboard plant cannot be repossessed if orders from electronics firms fall, and Bryn Dunmore keeps full control of the expansion. No lender can impose covenants on the eco-friendly ink strategy, which suits an autocratic founder running a flat structure. Using reserves also avoids loan-approval delays, so printing defects can be tackled with the new presses sooner and the 25,000-unit quarterly output protected.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation applied to the named business.

questions.question_text: Consider print media advertising, direct mail to purchasers, or social media campaigns. Which should DPC choose to promote its eco-friendly cartons? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Print media advertising: Trade and business press can reach the 550 purchasers surveyed and other packaging buyers with a credible message about eco-friendly inks. Costs are moderate and the message persists, but print cannot show the carton finish, has a long lead time and is weak at converting the 63% willing to pay $0.40 more into quick orders for the 100,000-unit target.

Direct mail to purchasers: Personalised mailings to known food and electronics firms can highlight the 49% who check packaging credentials and include physical samples, giving a tangible demonstration of the new cartons. Production and postage costs per contact are high, response rates are low, and a 100-staff business funding an $840,000 line must watch the budget carefully.

Social media campaigns: Targeted posts can show the eco-friendly ink story and recycled credentials to purchasing managers at low cost with measurable engagement, and content can be updated fast. However, corporate buyers may rely more on samples and existing relationships than on social feeds, so online interest alone may not secure large carton contracts.

Recommendation: DPC should choose social media campaigns supported by sample packs mailed to key purchasers. Social media reaches the 63% value segment cheaply and nationally, while samples supply the physical proof that social posts lack. Print media is rejected as slow and unable to demonstrate the $0.40 eco-friendly premium; broad direct mail is rejected as expensive and low-response, so targeted samples replace blanket mailings. With a $480,000 loan to service, keeping promotional spend proportionate to the $6.00 contribution per carton is essential for DPC.

mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of DPC with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options in the context of DPC with a well-justified recommendation explaining why print and blanket direct mail are rejected.

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for DPC of using job rotation to reduce its printing defect rate and late-delivery complaints.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Job rotation moves the 100 staff between printing presses, quality checks and dispatch, so workers understand how their own task affects the 2.9% defect rate and the 16 monthly late-delivery complaints. A press operator who has worked in dispatch is more aware of deadlines, while a checker who has run the presses spots printing faults earlier, reducing waste and protecting the $6.00 contribution per carton and the $840,000 investment.

Point 2: Rotation reduces repetition and broadens skills, raising motivation in a flat structure and giving cover when staff are absent. This is useful while 24 staff still lack training on the new printing presses, because rotated workers can support them and the $950 college courses can be focused on the hardest tasks. Higher flexibility helps meet the 100,000-unit annual target and the deliveries to food and electronics firms that Bryn Dunmore relies on, underlining the $840,000 investment and keeping the 2.9% defect rate under control.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation applied to the named business.

questions.question_text: Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college for the 24 staff. Which should DPC choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching at the printing presses is specific to DPC's own equipment, costs no fees and keeps the 24 staff productive while learning, protecting the 25,000 cartons made last quarter and the fall to a 2.9% defect rate. Its weaknesses are that mentor-operators lose time, bad habits can spread, and there is no formal certificate if food and electronics firms require proof of competence.

Off-the-job training: A local college course at $950 per employee provides structured skills and a recognised certificate for all 24 staff, costing $22,800 in total — modest against the $840,000 line. However, it removes 24 of 100 staff from production, cutting capacity when 100,000 cartons are needed, and the generic syllabus may not match DPC's presses, so on-site follow-up would still be required.

Decision: DPC should choose on-the-job training first, adding short college modules for supervisors later. It is cheaper, press-specific and avoids losing output while printing defects and late deliveries are active problems; full off-the-job training is rejected because releasing 24 staff and spending $22,800 would disrupt deliveries to key accounts, and formal certification can be built in once the new line is stable.

Additional considerations: The reduction in late-delivery complaints from 37 to 16 a month shows dispatch reliability is improving, and pulling 24 of 100 staff away for college could reverse this just as the $840,000 line starts. DPC could phase the $950 courses in small groups so printing and dispatch stay staffed, combining formal certification with immediate on-press practice and protecting the 100,000-carton target and key food and electronics accounts.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to DPC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods in the context of DPC.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods in the context of DPC with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and equipment relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how DPC's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 50,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $6.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 100,000-unit output; pricing and discount modelling against $300,000 fixed costs; loan feasibility for the $840,000 line; and unit cost of $10.50 with productivity of 1,000 units per worker, used to reduce the 2.9% defect rate.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $300,000 ÷ ($13.50 − $7.50) = $300,000 ÷ $6.00 = 50,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 50,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $13.50 − $7.50 = $6.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $6.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways DPC's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 50,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 100,000 units, a margin of safety of 50,000 units, to justify the $840,000 recycled-cardboard line.
2. Contribution of $6.00 lets managers test a purchaser discount: a $0.40 concession leaves $5.60 per carton, showing the extra volume needed to cover $300,000 fixed costs.
3. Fixed costs and contribution set the output required to service the $480,000 bank loan before further capital spending.
4. Unit cost of $300,000 ÷ 100,000 + $7.50 = $10.50 and productivity of 100,000 ÷ 100 = 1,000 units per worker allow weekly benchmarking and help cut the 2.9% printing defect rate.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate DPC's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Which ratio provides the stronger evidence of improvement? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 30.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 34.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 15.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 18.0%
ROCE 2024 = 18.0%
ROCE 2025 = 21.0%

Detailed workings: In 2024 gross profit of $1,620,000 = revenue $5,400,000 − cost of sales $3,780,000; $1,620,000 ÷ $5,400,000 = 30.0%. In 2025 gross profit of $2,142,000 = revenue $6,300,000 − cost of sales $4,158,000; $2,142,000 ÷ $6,300,000 = 34.0%. Operating profit rose from $810,000 to $1,134,000; $810,000 ÷ $5,400,000 = 15.0% and $1,134,000 ÷ $6,300,000 = 18.0%. Capital employed moved from $4,500,000 to $5,400,000; $810,000 ÷ $4,500,000 = 18.0% and $1,134,000 ÷ $5,400,000 = 21.0%. Interest payable was $105,000 then $135,000.

Evaluation: All three measures improved, so DPC's profitability strengthened. Gross profitability rose from 30.0% to 34.0%, consistent with better control of pulp and ink costs as the 2.9% defect rate fell. The operating return on sales improved from 15.0% to 18.0%, showing the $300,000 fixed costs are absorbed by output of 100,000 cartons. Return on capital rose from 18.0% to 21.0% despite capital employed reaching $5,400,000 to fund the $840,000 plant, so the new assets are earning.

Stronger evidence: the profit margin, because it gained three percentage points directly from the given revenue and operating profit and is not inflated by a smaller capital base, which also shapes the return on capital figure.

Conclusion: DPC's financial performance has improved across all three measures. The operating return on sales is the clearest indicator of efficiency; the caution is the $480,000 loan and rising interest payable, which must be covered from the stronger margins.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years, detailed evaluation of revenue, cost and capital movements, and a justified conclusion naming the stronger evidence.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for DPC of using eco-friendly inks and recycled cardboard in its cartons.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Eco-friendly inks and recycled cardboard match the 63% of 550 purchasers who would pay $0.40 more, letting DPC defend its $6.00 contribution per unit while pulp and ink input costs rise 9.8%. The 49% who check packaging credentials make the change a useful way to win and retain food and electronics contracts, supporting the $13.50 price and the $840,000 investment.

Disadvantage: Eco-friendly inks and recycled board can cost more or print less cleanly, which would raise the $7.50 variable cost per unit and squeeze margins unless the full $0.40 premium is secured. Poorer print quality could worsen the 2.9% defect rate or the 16 late-delivery complaints if suppliers are slower, adding cost while the $480,000 bank loan still needs servicing. With $360,000 of retained profit tied up in the $840,000 line, the $6.00 contribution must also cover that loan, leaving little room for any rise in the $7.50 variable cost per carton.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation applied to the named business.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 9.8% rise in paper pulp and eco-ink input costs will affect DPC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Base interest rate (4.5% to 5.25%): If DPC's $480,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage point rise adds 0.0075 × $480,000 = $3,600 a year. That is small against $300,000 of fixed costs, and zero if the loan is fixed-rate. Higher base rates could raise future borrowing costs and make purchasers cautious, but DPC can cap the direct risk by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage (6.4%, to $14.10 from $13.25 per hour): With a workforce of 100 in printing and dispatch, this feeds into wage bills and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay rates, so a total wage bill cannot be honestly invented; the defensible test is productivity of 100,000 units ÷ 100 staff = 1,000 units per worker. If productivity holds, the rise is absorbable; if it slips, unit labour costs rise and the $6.00 contribution narrows.

Input cost inflation (9.8% pulp and eco-inks): The insert does not decompose the $7.50 variable cost, so only a bound can be stated: if all of it rose 9.8%, that adds 9.8% × $7.50 = $0.74 per unit; across 100,000 cartons that is about $73,500 a year (100,000 × $0.735). The $0.40 eco-friendly premium can recover only part of this, while packaged-goods spending grew just 2.2%.

Conclusion: The 9.8% input-cost rise has the greatest impact because it applies to every one of the 100,000 cartons and directly erodes the $6.00 contribution supporting the $840,000 line. The interest effect is modest and fixable, and the wage rise can be offset if productivity holds, whereas input inflation attacks unit economics with little pricing room.
